title: Three newspapers and 90 readers
intro: A survey of 90 residents of a housing society asked which of three newspapers, Daily, Weekly and Monthly, they read. 58 residents read the Daily, 51 read the Weekly and 47 read the Monthly.
clues: Every resident reads at least one of the three newspapers.

questions.stem: What is the greatest possible number of residents who read all three newspapers?
why: With n1, n2 and t reading exactly one, two and three papers: n1 + n2 + t = 90 and n1 + 2n2 + 3t = 58 + 51 + 47 = 156. Subtracting, n2 + 2t = 66, so t is at most 33.
33 works: 25 only Daily, 18 only Weekly, 14 only Monthly and 33 all three.

questions.stem: What is the least possible number of residents who read exactly one newspaper?
why: From the two equations, n1 = 90 − t − (66 − 2t) = 24 + t, which is least when t = 0.
24 works: 24 only Weekly, 19 Daily and Weekly, 39 Daily and Monthly, 8 Weekly and Monthly.

questions.stem: If exactly 25 residents read exactly one newspaper, how many read exactly two?
why: n1 = 24 + t = 25 gives t = 1, and then n2 = 66 − 2 = 64.

questions.stem: If every resident who reads the Monthly also reads at least one other newspaper, what is the greatest possible number of residents who read exactly one newspaper?
why: Nobody reads only the Monthly, so all 90 read the Daily or the Weekly, and 58 + 51 − 90 = 19 read both. Anyone reading all three reads both, so t is at most 19.
Then n1 = 24 + t is at most 43, reached with 11 only Daily, 32 only Weekly, 28 Daily and Monthly, and 19 all three.

questions.stem: What is the least possible number of residents who read both the Daily and the Weekly?
why: At most 90 read the Daily or the Weekly, so at least 58 + 51 − 90 = 19 read both.
19 works: 39 only Daily, 4 Daily and Weekly only, 32 Weekly and Monthly only, 15 all three.

steps: Let n1, n2 and t be the numbers reading exactly one, exactly two and all three. Everyone reads at least one, so nobody is outside the circles: n1 + n2 + t = 90.
Adding the three readerships counts each resident once per paper read: n1 + 2n2 + 3t = 156. Subtracting, n2 + 2t = 66, so n1 = 24 + t.
So t is at most 33 (when n2 = 0) and n1 at least 24. The picture shows the case with the most readers of all three; each question adds one more equation or bound.

diagram.note: Counts of residents in each region; t is the number reading all three.

title: Four games and 120 members
sub: four sets, exactly and at least
intro: A club has 120 members. 80 members play Chess, 70 play Carrom, 60 play Ludo and 50 play Cards.
clues: Each member plays at least two of the four games.

questions.stem: What is the greatest possible number of members who play all four games?
why: With n2, n3, n4 playing exactly two, three and four games: n2 + n3 + n4 = 120 and 2n2 + 3n3 + 4n4 = 260, so n3 + 2n4 = 20 and n4 is at most 10.
10 works: 10 play all four, and 20 Chess and Carrom, 20 Chess and Ludo, 30 Chess and Cards, 30 Carrom and Ludo, 10 Carrom and Cards play just those two.

questions.stem: What is the greatest possible number of members who play exactly three games?
why: From n3 + 2n4 = 20, n3 is largest when n4 = 0: 20.
For example 20 Chess and Carrom, 40 Chess and Ludo, 40 Carrom and Cards, 10 Chess, Carrom and Ludo, and 10 Chess, Ludo and Cards.

questions.stem: What is the least possible number of members who play at least three games?
why: n3 + n4 = 20 − n4, least when n4 is largest, 10. So 10.

questions.stem: What is the least possible number of members who play both Chess and Carrom?
why: Let m members play neither Chess nor Carrom; they play exactly Ludo and Cards. Those playing Chess or Carrom number 120 − m, so both: 80 + 70 − (120 − m) = 30 + m.
Least at m = 0: 30.

questions.stem: If no member plays both Ludo and Cards, how many members play exactly two games?
why: Anyone playing all four plays Ludo and Cards, so n4 = 0. Then n3 = 20 and n2 = 120 − 20 = 100.

steps: Nobody plays fewer than two games. Let n2, n3, n4 play exactly two, three and four: n2 + n3 + n4 = 120.
Counting each member once per game played: 2n2 + 3n3 + 4n4 = 80 + 70 + 60 + 50 = 260. Subtract twice the first: n3 + 2n4 = 20.
Every 'exactly' and 'at least' question follows from n3 + 2n4 = 20; a question about two particular games uses the members outside both.

diagram.note: Each member is counted once per game played in the game totals.

title: Five judges pick favourites
intro: Five judges each secretly picked exactly three of six contestants, P, Q, R, S, T and U, as their favourites. The number of judges who picked each contestant (the votes) is in the table. Nothing else is known.
clues: A judge's pick is a set of three different contestants.
Two judges may have made the same pick.

questions.stem: What is the greatest possible number of judges who picked exactly the trio P, Q and R?
why: Every judge picked P and nobody picked U. R has 3 votes, so at most 3 judges have P, Q and R.
3 is reached in the collection PQR, PQR, PQR, PQS, PST.

questions.stem: Ignoring which judge made which pick, how many different collections of five picks are consistent with the votes?
why: Exactly one judge skipped Q and picked two of R, S, T; the other four picked Q and one of R, S, T.
If the non-Q judge picked S and T: PQR ×3, PQS, PST. R and T: PQR ×2, PQS ×2, PRT. R and S: PQR ×2, PQS, PQT, PRS. Three collections.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
options: Some judge picked both R and S.
At least two judges picked exactly P, Q and R.
Some judge picked both Q and T.
At least two judges picked both Q and S.
why: P, Q, R appears 3, 2 and 2 times in the three collections, so at least twice always.
R with S, and Q with T, appear only in the third collection; two picks with Q and S appear only in the second.

questions.stem: If some judge picked both R and S, how many judges picked both Q and R?
why: Only the collection PQR, PQR, PQS, PQT, PRS has a pick with R and S. In it, Q and R appear together in the two copies of PQR.

questions.stem: What is the greatest possible number of different picks (distinct sets of three contestants) among the five judges?
why: The first two collections have 3 distinct picks each; PQR, PQR, PQS, PQT, PRS has 4. The greatest is 4.

steps: P has 5 votes, so every judge picked P; U has 0, so nobody did. Each judge picked two more from Q, R, S and T, and those 10 places give Q 4, R 3, S 2, T 1.
Q has 4 votes, so exactly one judge left Q out and picked two of R, S, T; the other four picked Q and one of R, S, T.
Try each pair for the non-Q judge. S and T, R and T, or R and S each leave exactly one way to fill the rest: three collections, and every question reads off them.

rows: Non-Q judge picked S and T
Non-Q judge picked R and T
Non-Q judge picked R and S
diagram.note: One row for each choice of the judge who left Q out.
frames: P + two of Q, R, S, T
P + two of Q, R, S, T
P + two of Q, R, S, T

title: A four-language school
intro: A school has 100 students. 60 study English, 50 study Hindi, 40 study French and 25 study German.
clues: Every student studies at least one of the four languages.
Every student who studies German also studies French.
Exactly 30 students study only one language.

questions.stem: What is the greatest possible number of students who study exactly three languages?
why: 5 works: 25 only English, 5 only Hindi, 30 English and Hindi, 10 Hindi and French, 5 English, Hindi and French, 25 French and German.

questions.stem: What is the least possible number of students who study exactly two languages?
What is the least possible number of students who study only English?
why: The 60 students without French cannot study German, so each studies only English (a), only Hindi (b) or exactly English and Hindi (c): a + b + c = 60. With a + b + f = 30 (f only French), c = 30 + f.
Hindi needs b + c ≤ 50, so b + f ≤ 20 and a = 30 − (b + f) ≥ 10. 10 is reached.

questions.stem: If exactly 2 students study all four languages, what is the greatest possible number of students who study only Hindi?
why: The 2 who study all four also study Hindi, so b + c + 2 ≤ 50. With c = 30 + f, b + f ≤ 18, so b ≤ 18.
18 is reached: 12 only English, 18 only Hindi, 30 English and Hindi, 15 English and French, 22 French and German, 1 English, French and German, 2 all four.

questions.stem: If no student studies both English and German, how many students study exactly three languages?
why: A student of all four would study English and German, so n4 = 0, and n3 + 2n4 = 5 gives n3 = 5.

steps: Nobody studies German without French, so nobody studies only German, and the 60 students without French cannot study German either: each of them studies only English, only Hindi, or exactly English and Hindi.
With 30 on one language: n2 + n3 + n4 = 70, and counting each student once per language, 2n2 + 3n3 + 4n4 = 175 − 30 = 145. Subtract twice the first: n3 + 2n4 = 5.
Let a, b, f study only English, only Hindi, only French, and c exactly English and Hindi. Then a + b + f = 30 and a + b + c = 60, so c = 30 + f, which ties the English and Hindi counts to the rest.

diagram.note: Each student is counted once per language studied in the language totals.

title: The sports group
intro: A group has between 41 and 79 people. Exactly half of them watch Cricket, two-fifths watch Football and one-third watch Tennis. One-tenth of the group watch none of these three sports.
clues: Every count is a whole number of people.

questions.stem: How many people are there in the group?
why: Half, two-fifths, one-third and one-tenth must all be whole, so the size is a multiple of 2, 5, 3 and 10, that is of 30. From 41 to 79 that is 60.

questions.stem: What is the greatest possible number of people who watch all three sports?
why: With 60: Cricket 30, Football 24, Tennis 20, none 6, so 54 watch at least one. n1 + n2 + n3 = 54 and n1 + 2n2 + 3n3 = 74 give n2 + 2n3 = 20: n3 is at most 10.
10 works: 10 all three, 20 only Cricket, 14 only Football, 10 only Tennis, 6 none.

questions.stem: What is the least possible number of people who watch exactly one of the three sports?
why: n1 = 54 − n2 − n3 = 34 + n3, least at n3 = 0: 34 (30 only Cricket, 4 only Football, 20 Football and Tennis, 6 none).

questions.stem: If nobody watches both Cricket and Tennis, how many people watch only Football?
why: The 30 Cricket and 20 Tennis watchers are different people: 50. Of the 54 who watch something, the other 4 watch only Football.

questions.stem: If exactly 5 people watch all three sports, what is the greatest possible number of people who watch only Football?
why: The 24 Football watchers include the 5 who watch all three, so at most 19 watch only Football.
19 works: 5 all three, 19 only Football, 15 only Cricket, 5 only Tennis, 10 Cricket and Tennis, 6 none.

steps: Whole-number counts fix the size first: it must be a multiple of 2, 5, 3 and 10, that is of 30, so 60.
With 60: Cricket 30, Football 24, Tennis 20 and 6 watch none, so 54 watch at least one.
With n1, n2, n3 watching exactly one, two and three: n1 + n2 + n3 = 54 and n1 + 2n2 + 3n3 = 74, so n2 + 2n3 = 20. The picture shows the most who can watch all three.

diagram.note: Counts of people in each region.
